articles.title: Solved: The Web Has Native Partials. Introducing the Remote Module Definition Pattern.
articles.excerpt: TL;DR, The Discovery. For decades, web developers have complained about the lack of native, zero-dependency browser partials and serverless includes. We were told we needed heavy third-party framework…
articles.body: TL;DR, The Discovery. For decades, web developers have complained about the lack of native, zero-dependency browser partials and serverless includes. We were told we needed heavy third-party framework compilation layers just to slice code layout efficiently. We were told wrong. The Remote Module Definition (RMD) pattern removes this bottleneck natively inside the browser’s raw engine. By returning to first principles, we have turned the web into an open plugin architecture — eliminating framework technical debt, restoring data sovereignty, and setting the baseline for entirely new web architectures and new web markets.
articles.author: cScarlson

articles.title: Free Uptime Monitoring Tools for Web Application Scheduled Imports
articles.excerpt: The right free monitor depends on which failure you need to catch. For a web application's public endpoint, Uptime Robot or StatusCake is the practical starting point. For a scheduled import that stop…
articles.body: The right free monitor depends on which failure you need to catch. For a web application's public endpoint, Uptime Robot or StatusCake is the practical starting point. For a scheduled import that stops producing records while the homepage stays green, add a heartbeat-style check such as Healthchecks. A metrics platform can help you build the missing signal, but it is a different trade-off: more control, more polling code, and more responsibility for notification delivery. TL;DR: use a dedicated free uptime monitor for reachability, a job heartbeat for silent schedule failures, and a unified observability API only when you are willing to assemble the alert loop yourself. Free plans commonly check every 5 minutes and keep SMS, webhook notifications, or richer reporting behind paid features.

articles.title: How We Made Magic and Technology Clash Using Bluetooth
articles.excerpt: Building a BLE-based aura system for a live-action role-playing game It all started with a plan for a live-action role-playing game (LARP) inspired by Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura, a comp…
articles.body: Building a BLE-based aura system for a live-action role-playing game It all started with a plan for a live-action role-playing game (LARP) inspired by Arcanum: Of Steamworks and Magick Obscura , a computer RPG set in a world where magic and technology coexist but fundamentally clash. In our game, this conflict was supposed to manifest itself through auras. A mage would radiate a magical aura capable of disrupting nearby machinery. technology, in turn, would interfere with magic. But we didn't want this to be just another rule that players had to act out. We wanted the conflict to have a real, physical effect: a player could walk up to a working machine and cause it to stop.

articles.body: 📅 November 5, 2026 • NVIDIA NVIDIA has released four open-weight Cosmos 3 Nano checkpoints for interactive world simulation, per the NVIDIA blog on Hugging Face on November 5, 2026. The checkpoints target two domains where world models are becoming working infrastructure: driving and robotics . The weights are hosted on Hugging Face , and alongside them NVIDIA published post-training recipes and coding-agent skills — material meant to help teams adapt the models to their own sensor rigs and robot embodiments. Two named variants cover complementary tasks. Transfer-Auto turns a scenario into synchronized multi-sensor data, generating up to 11 camera views — including fisheye — with joint RGB-LiDAR generation , so camera and LiDAR outputs stay consistent within one pass.

articles.title: 'We got it done!' Spacewalking astronauts finish installing next-gen ISS solar arrays
articles.excerpt: Spacewalkers Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk installed the final ISS Roll-Out Solar Array on Thursday (Nov. 5), wrapping up a multiyear effort to boost the station's power generation by 30%.
articles.body: Just as NASA is preparing to demonstrate " Max Power " on the ground, two astronauts on a spacewalk have provided the International Space Station (ISS) with the same. Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency installed and deployed the eighth and final ISS Roll-Out Solar Array (iROSA) on Thursday (Nov. 5), augmenting the space station's legacy solar array wings to produce as much as 30% more electricity. "We got it done!" said Menon at the end of the 6-hour-and-59-minute spacewalk . The EVA (extravehicular activity) began at 8:36 a.m. EST and ended at 3:35 p.m. EST (1336 to 2035 GMT).

articles.title: Earth has captured a new mini moon  — but it won't stick around for long
articles.excerpt: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and QQ8 is sticking around for Christmas.
articles.body: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and it is sticking around for Christmas. The space rock, designated 2026 QQ8, was first observed in August 2026 after entering orbit around Earth in April 2026. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on Thursday (Oct. 29). The stay of QQ8 is a temporary one. The mini-moon will remain in the thrall of Earth's gravity through December before breaking away in 2027. Scientists have recreated the orbital path of QQ8, finding that it takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year, to orbit the sun . QQ8 closely approaches Earth around once every ten years, but this time the object came so close that Earth has been able to gravitationally seize it.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 5, 2002: NASA's Galileo spacecraft flies by Jupiter moon Amalthea only to find it's a 'pile of icy rubble less dense than water'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft flew by a small moon called Amalthea and made a surprising find. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 5, 2002, NASA's old Galileo spacecraft was almost out of fuel. But the Jupiter mission still had some science to do. Galileo flew by a small moon called Amalthea. Amalthea is small, but it's interesting for scientists. The Jupiter moon Amalthea is the reddest object in our solar system. It also generates more heat than it gets from the sun. Scientists think Amalthea creates electrical currents as it orbits in Jupiter's huge magnetic field. Near this little moon, strong radiation from Jupiter is dangerous for spacecraft. The flyby caused some problems for Galileo. The spacecraft went into safe mode only 30 minutes after going past Amalthea. NASA said it was ready for problems, because Galileo was on its last legs, and the radiation near Amalthea was strong.
